youtube.title: How Touchscreens Work (Why Your Finger Works but Gloves Don't)
youtube.summary: Your phone screen does not feel your finger press. It feels the tiny bit of electrical charge your finger steals. In this video we look at the invisible grid of wires inside a touchscreen, how a controller chip finds the exact spot you touched, why gloves and water confuse it, how old resistive screens were different, and how touchscreens went from a 1965 radar lab to every pocket.
youtube.details:
Key facts (checked November 2026):
- Projected capacitive screens use a grid of transparent electrodes over the display; a touch changes the capacitance and a controller works out the position (Newhaven Display)
- Capacitive screens need bare skin, a conductive stylus or special gloves, and are sensitive to moisture; resistive screens work with gloves because they use pressure (Newhaven Display)
- Resistive screens: two layers coated with indium tin oxide, separated by spacer dots (Newhaven Display)
- History: E.A. Johnson, Royal Radar Establishment, 1965; Samuel Hurst resistive 1971, transparent 1974; Frank Beck and Bent Stumpe at CERN, 1973; IBM Simon, 1994; LG Prada and iPhone capacitive phones, 2006-2007 (Newhaven Display, Wikipedia)
- Touch sampling rates on phones are commonly 120 Hz or higher

shorts.headline: How your phone finds your finger
Why gloves don't work on phones
The touchscreen is older than you think

scenes.chapterTitle: Intro: a screen that feels you
scenes.badge: Many phones check for your finger
scenes.sub: or more, looking for tiny changes in charge
scenes.text: You tap, swipe and pinch your phone screen hundreds of times a day, and it almost never misses. But your screen cannot actually feel pressure the way your skin does. Instead, it is watching for something much stranger, the tiny bit of electricity in your body. Many phones check the screen one hundred and twenty times or more every second, looking for your finger. In this video we will see the invisible grid hidden under the glass, how your phone works out the exact spot you touched, why it ignores your gloves, and how this idea started in a radar lab back in the nineteen sixties.

items.text: The screen holds a tiny electric field
Your finger pulls a little charge away

scenes.text: Here is the key idea. Your body is mostly salty water, and salty water conducts electricity. The glass on your phone has a weak electric field spread across it, far too small for you to feel. When your finger comes close, it pulls a little of that charge away, a bit like a sponge soaking up a drop of water. Nothing flows through you in a way you could ever notice, and it is completely safe. But the screen can measure that tiny change. It notices the missing charge, and that is how it knows a finger has arrived. This is called capacitive sensing.

So what is actually under the glass? At the top is the tough cover glass, the part you touch. Just under it, or built right into the display, is the sensor, a grid of very thin lines arranged in rows and columns. They are made from a special material, often indium tin oxide, that conducts electricity but is almost completely transparent. That is why you can see the picture straight through it. Below that is the display itself, which makes the image. And connected to the grid is a small controller chip, whose only job is to read the grid, over and over, and report where it is being touched.

scenes.chapterTitle: How the grid finds your finger

items.text: Rows send out a tiny signal
A finger weakens it at one crossing

scenes.text: Here is how the grid finds you. The controller sends a tiny signal down one row at a time. Every column listens to see how much of that signal comes across. Where a row and a column cross, they form a tiny sensor. Normally each crossing passes the same amount of signal. But when your finger is close, it steals some of the charge, so the signal at that crossing becomes weaker. The chip scans every row, checks every column, and builds a map of where the signal dropped. The spot with the biggest drop is your finger. It turns that into a position, and sends it to the phone.

items.title: Self capacitance
items.sub: fast, but two fingers can confuse it

scenes.text: There are two main ways to read the grid. In self capacitance, the chip checks each whole row and each whole column on its own. It is fast and sensitive, but with two fingers it can get confused, because it only knows which rows and which columns changed, not exactly which crossings. That can create ghost touches. In mutual capacitance, the chip measures every single crossing separately. So it can see two, five, or even ten fingers at once, each in its own place. That is what makes pinch to zoom possible. Most phones use mutual sensing, and many mix in self sensing for extra sensitivity.

But wait, the lines in the grid are spaced apart, so how can your phone be so precise? The trick is that your fingertip is wider than the gap between lines. So a single touch covers several crossings at once, each one changed by a different amount. The crossing right under the centre of your finger changes the most, and the ones at the edge change less. The chip averages these values to find the true centre of your touch, which can be between lines, not just on them. Then software smooths the path as you move, so your swipe draws a clean line instead of a shaky one.

scenes.chapterTitle: Why gloves and water confuse it
scenes.text: This also explains some everyday annoyances. Normal gloves are made of wool, leather or plastic, which do not conduct electricity. So your charge cannot reach the screen, and nothing happens. Special touchscreen gloves have conductive thread sewn into the fingertips, which carries your charge through. Water is the opposite problem. Drops of water also conduct, so a wet screen can register fake touches or jump around. And if you tap with the tip of your fingernails, the phone often ignores you, because nails do not conduct well. A stylus for a phone works only because its tip is made of a conductor too.

items.title: You press
items.sub: where they meet is the spot

scenes.text: Older touchscreens worked in a completely different way. They are called resistive screens, and you can still find them on some ticket machines and factory equipment. They have two flexible layers, each coated with a thin conductor, held apart by tiny spacer dots. When you press, the top layer bends down and touches the bottom one. The controller measures the electricity where they meet to find the spot. The upside is that you can use almost anything, gloves, a pen, or a stick. The downside is that you have to press harder, they usually handle only one touch at a time, and the picture looks less clear.

scenes.chapterTitle: From a radar lab to your pocket
scenes.text: The idea is older than most people think. In nineteen sixty five, E. A. Johnson, an engineer at the Royal Radar Establishment in Britain, built the first finger driven touchscreen, using capacitance, for air traffic control. In nineteen seventy three, engineers at CERN in Switzerland built a see through capacitive touchscreen to control their equipment. In nineteen ninety four, the IBM Simon became one of the first phones with a touchscreen, though you used a stylus and a resistive screen. Then around two thousand seven, the LG Prada and the iPhone brought capacitive multi touch screens to the mass market. Today, that radar lab idea lives in billions of pockets.

Finding the touch is only half the job. Software has to decide what that touch means. It uses palm rejection, so when the side of your hand brushes the screen while you hold your phone, it does not count as a tap. It recognises gestures, like a quick swipe, a slow drag, a long press or a two finger pinch, by watching how the touch points move over time. And some gaming phones scan the screen even faster, so your taps register a little sooner. The hardware finds where you touched. The software works out the meaning, and that is what makes it feel natural.

items.text: A see-through grid holds a tiny charge
Your finger steals some at one crossing
A chip maps it, software reads it

scenes.text: Let us recap in three points. One. Under the glass there is a transparent grid of rows and columns holding a tiny electric charge. Two. Because your body conducts, your finger steals a little of that charge at the crossings beneath it. Three. A controller chip maps those changes many times a second, and software turns them into taps, swipes and pinches. So every time you touch your phone, your finger quite literally becomes part of the circuit.

scenes.title: How touchscreens work
scenes.text: So the next time your phone ignores you because you are wearing gloves, you will know exactly why. It is not being stubborn. It simply cannot feel your charge. Now I want to hear from you. Have you ever had a phone screen go crazy in the rain? Tell me in the comments. If you enjoyed this, subscribe to Tech Explained. In the next video, we will look at Starlink, and how internet can come from satellites flying above your head.
